pr_body:
It's not really clear exactly how we run into a conflict, we'd
need to pick the same expiration as an already existing lease but
not the same as the current lease. This means that the lease which
we conflict with must be in the process of being dropped. We'll
handle the edge case, but I'm not sure how to test whether it
happens in practice.

Fixes #78479.

Release note: None

comments:
@stevendanna @rhu713 
Is this the result of the new index backfiller? Is this a known issue?

```
        	            	lease-insert: duplicate key value violates unique constraint "primary"
```

I can take a deeper dive to be sure. But on first glance my guess is that it isn't related to the index backfiller.  That duplicate key violation appears to be happening here:

https://github.com/cockroachdb/cockroach/blob/ca927f04be3dcb6d8bd682860e02423b7d42648e/pkg/sql/catalog/lease/storage.go#L150-L162

On a system table that I don't think should have had any index-backfiller interactions.  The test itself is doing column additions and drops which should use the column backfiller rather than the index backfiller.

I think this is an extreme edge-case whereby we remove the old leases asynchronously and then we go to acquire a fresh lease but the jitter happens to be such that they overlap. It seems shockingly rare, but we can easily retry. I'll deal with it. The testing is going to be the annoying part.
manually reviewed and brought up to date

review_comments: Couldn't we instead salt the least significant bits of the jittered expiration timestamp somehow to prevent collisions?

The expiration timestamp is guaranteed to be unique for that node and since that's part of the PK we won't ever be inserting duplicate rows.

I'm obviously misunderstanding something here but I have no idea what.

We're already jittering randomly by 5%. The hazard is that the same node picks a timestamp which is now + 5m +/- 5% and then releases it and then picks another one and it happens to be the same. This is a ~1/5M conflict (we store leases at microsecond resolution). Seems very very rare. Maybe there's something else going on, but I couldn't spot it.

This matches my understanding. I was suggesting we maintain a global `var jitterCounter int64` with which we call `jitteredLeaseDuration(atomic.AddInt64(&jitterCounter, 1))` which salts the timestamp somehow, perhaps by overwriting the least significant 20 bits.

I took a bit more time to see how `rand.Float64` works and it seems exceedingly unlikely that collisions would occur unless `descriptor_lease_duration` and `descriptor_lease_jitter_fraction` were set to ridiculous values, which doesn't appear to be the case. The random number generator's internal state is protected by a mutex so each call to `rand.Float64` should generate a unique-enough value regardless of concurrency.

> we store leases at microsecond resolution

I didn't notice this. This changes things. I was assuming a nanosecond resolution.
So, the likelihood of a collision would be on the order or one in ten million: "rare but not rare enough" sounds about right to me.
